title: Shell Scripting
learningGoals: Explain what the shell and a shell script are, why scripts exist, and where they're used (DevOps, data science, security, AI/ML).
Write and run scripts that use command-line arguments ( $1 , $# , $0 ), read , expr and arithmetic.
Use system/environment variables vs user-defined variables correctly (no spaces around = ).
Write conditions with test / [ ] (numeric, string and file tests), if , if-else , elif , nested if , and case .
Write for (list style and C style) and while loops with break and continue .
Handle files (copy lines N..M) two ways, and use arrays (length, slice, replace, unset).
Solve classic programs: reverse a number, perfect number, number pattern, even/odd, sum of digits, menu calculator, palindromes in a file.
Apply hard links vs soft links to scenarios.
sirStressed: "Shell scripting saves time and reduces errors": write it once, fix it once, reuse it forever.
Shift your thinking from typing commands to composing workflows. Small commands are LEGO blocks.

Exam questions are scenario-based, use-case-based and application-based. "We will never ask you to write a very lengthy script." "We don't test your memory; we test solid understanding, application and problem-solving."
Using AI to write scripts is fine, but understand every line, test it and cross-check the output. Ask the AI to comment each line.
Hands-on is a must. Use WSL on Windows; macOS works out of the box.
A hard link is not a copy. It's one more name for the same inode, and the file is gone only when the link count reaches 0. A soft link can point to network files; a hard link can't.
commonTraps: Spaces around = ( a = 5 ) cause an error. Write a=5 .
Forgetting spaces inside the test brackets: [$a -gt 5] is wrong; [ $a -gt 5 ] is right.
Using > or < for numbers inside [ ] . Use -gt / -lt ; inside [ ] , > means redirection.
expr $a * $b without the backslash. It must be \* .
Thinking 0 means false. In the shell, exit status 0 = true/success.
Ending if with end or } . It's fi ; case ends with esac ; loops use do … done .
Forgetting to increment in a while loop gives an infinite loop.
Using single quotes instead of backticks around expr . Single quotes print the text literally.
summary: Shell = translator between you and the OS. Script = commands in a file that run in sequence, like a batch. It saves time and reduces errors. Not for GUIs.
Run with sh file.sh , or chmod +x then ./file.sh . #!/bin/bash is the shebang; # is a comment.
$0 (script name), $1 .. (arguments), $# (count), $@ (all), $? (exit status). read var takes input.
`expr $a + $b` : backticks, \* for multiplication, integer only. $(( )) is the modern form.
Variables are untyped and case-sensitive; no spaces around = . System variables are UPPERCASE ( PATH , HOME , PWD , USER , SHELL ). export makes a variable environment-wide.
if … then … elif … else … fi ; case $v in pat) …;; *) …;; esac .
for i in list; do … done ; for (( i=0; i<n; i++ )) ; while [ cond ]; do … done ; break , continue .
Files: head -$end | tail -$num , or while read line … done < file .
Programs: reverse ( %10 , *10+ , /10 ), perfect number (divisors up to n/2), pattern (nested while, echo -n ), even/odd, digit sum, menu calculator, palindromes.
Links: hard = inode, same FS, survives deletion. Soft = path, can cross filesystems, dangles.

questions.prompt: Which wc option prints the length of the longest line?
questions.explanation: capital -L = longest line. Lowercase -l = line count, -w = words, -c = bytes.

questions.prompt: You want to copy lines 5 to 15 of a file. Which command is best suited?
questions.explanation: the idea is right: take the first 15 lines, then keep the last few. But lines 5–15 are 11 lines, so the exact command is head -15 file | tail -11 (or sed -n '5,15p' file ). Option A actually gives lines 6–15. Pick A in the quiz, but know the exact form. worked out.
topicTags: Text Processing Commands: Filters (wc, sort, head, tail)

questions.prompt: Piping follows ______ data flow from one command to the next.
questions.explanation: a pipe is a FIFO buffer. Data comes out in the same order it went in. worked out, not from the quiz review. The recorded flag on D was uncertain.

questions.prompt: Which grep option matches the whole line exactly?
questions.explanation: -x = the whole line must match. -w = whole word, -c = count, -i = ignore case.

questions.prompt: Which find command finds files with read-only permission for everyone (user, group, other)?
questions.explanation: 444 = r--r--r-- . Option A finds symlinks and B finds small files. D lacks the dash and uses 400 (user only).

questions.prompt: (i) A symbolic link acts like a shortcut. (ii) Deleting the file doesn't remove the data as long as at least one symbolic link remains.
questions.explanation: a symlink only stores the path. Delete the original and the link dangles, because the data is gone.
topicTags: File Processing Commands: Hard Link and Symbolic Link

questions.prompt: (i) Hard links can be created for directories. (ii) Deleting the file doesn't remove the data as long as at least one hard link to that inode remains.
questions.explanation: hard links to directories aren't allowed (they could create loops). The data lives until the inode's link count reaches 0.
topicTags: File Processing Commands: Hard Link and Symbolic Link

questions.prompt: What does this program do?
questions.code:
echo Enter two numbers with space in between
read a b
m=$a
if [ $b -lt $m ]; then m=$b; fi
while [ $m -ne 0 ]
do
     x=`expr $a % $m`
     y=`expr $b % $m`
     if [ $x -eq 0 -a $y -eq 0 ]; then
          echo Output of $a and $b is $m
          break
     fi
     m=`expr $m - 1`
done
questions.explanation: it counts down from the smaller number, and the first value that divides both is the greatest common divisor.

questions.prompt: Take one number (2–999) from the command line, with error checks, and say whether it's prime.
questions.code:
#!/bin/bash
if [ $# -ne 1 ]; then echo "Usage: $0 <number 2-999>"; exit 1; fi
n=$1
if [ $n -lt 2 -o $n -gt 999 ]; then echo "Number must be between 2 and 999"; exit 1; fi
i=2; prime=1
while [ `expr $i \* $i` -le $n ]
do
     if [ `expr $n % $i` -eq 0 ]; then prime=0; break; fi
     i=`expr $i + 1`
done
if [ $prime -eq 1 ]; then echo "$n is PRIME"; else echo "$n is NOT prime"; fi

questions.prompt: Read Num integers into an array, bubble-sort it, and display the result.
questions.code:
#!/bin/bash
echo "How many numbers?"; read n
for (( i=0; i<n; i++ )); do read -p "Element $((i+1)): " arr[$i]; done
for (( i=0; i<n-1; i++ ))
do
     for (( j=0; j<n-i-1; j++ ))
     do
          if [ ${arr[$j]} -gt ${arr[$((j+1))]} ]; then
               t=${arr[$j]}; arr[$j]=${arr[$((j+1))]}; arr[$((j+1))]=$t
          fi
     done
done
echo "Sorted: ${arr[@]}"

questions.prompt: Load an array from a file (the file name is a command-line argument) and find the second-largest number without sorting.
questions.code:
#!/bin/bash
if [ $# -ne 1 ] || [ ! -f "$1" ]; then echo "Usage: $0 <existing file>"; exit 1; fi
i=0
while read line; do arr[$i]=$line; i=`expr $i + 1`; done < "$1"
if [ ${#arr[@]} -lt 2 ]; then echo "Need at least 2 numbers"; exit 1; fi
first=${arr[0]}; second=""
for x in "${arr[@]:1}"
do
     if [ $x -gt $first ]; then second=$first; first=$x
     elif [ $x -ne $first ] && { [ -z "$second" ] || [ $x -gt $second ]; }; then second=$x
     fi
done
echo "Largest: $first    Second largest: ${second:-none (all equal)}"

questions.prompt: Every night you must copy all .log files from /var/app into a dated backup folder and delete the ones older than 7 days. Why is a shell script the right tool? Name two commands you'd use.
correctAnswers: The task is repetitive and scheduled, which is exactly what automation is for. A script saves time, avoids manual mistakes, and can run unattended from a scheduler. Commands: mkdir -p /backup/$(date +%F) , cp /var/app/*.log /backup/$(date +%F)/ , find /backup -mtime +7 -delete .

Commands: mkdir -p /backup/$(date +%F) , cp /var/app/*.log /backup/$(date +%F)/ , find /backup -mtime +7 -delete .

questions.prompt: Explain what happens to hard.txt and soft.txt after rm notes.txt in the live demo, and why.
correctAnswers: hard.txt still shows "Linux Learning", because it's another name for the same inode. The link count drops from 2 to 1, and the data is freed only at 0. soft.txt fails (it's dangling), because it stores only the path notes.txt , which no longer exists.
